excerpt_original: In her first monograph, published by Damiani, American photographer Lara Porzak brings together her tintypes and gelatin silver prints. Landscapes of the American West, horses, and still lifes compose a body of work against forgetting. L’article Lara Porzak, Alchemist of Memory…

blocks.text: Lightning strikes the Grand Canyon. Dated 1993, it is the oldest image in the book. A tintype allows no copy and forgives no mistake: the blackened iron sheet loaded into the camera comes out the other side as the image itself. “The present will become the past at the exact moment light strikes my film,” she warns. The process sets its own terms: fifteen minutes, no more. After that, the collodion dries and everything is lost.

She carries her darkroom into the field, into the canyons. “I want to remember the poetry of the moment I set up my tripod,” she writes. A hundred and sixty years before her, Timothy O’Sullivan and Carleton Watkins worked the same American West the same way — expedition gear loaded onto mule-drawn wagons. Porzak’s landscapes could almost have come back from that same journey, when the West was still a frontier.

“I want to remember my hopeful waiting as I pour the chemistry over the tin,” she adds. The emulsion reads blue and ultraviolet; red dies in it. The ochre earth of Red Earth, Arizona comes out pale as ash. A speck of dust, a shift in humidity, and the plate turns differently. She chose to keep the evidence of those accidents. A white veil has crept across nearly the entire valley of Spaceless Yosemite , and darkness has taken the edges of Our View, The Lake , narrowing the landscape to an oval of light. “Listen to the tin,” she breathes.

Horses surge through the pages from beginning to end. She draws close enough to let them spill past the frame. In Carrara , a neck and mane fill the entire space: the black is deep, the white creamy. Elsewhere, the face of a barn owl forms a heart, two dark eyes fixed on the lens. Butterflies are photographed head-on, motionless, the veins of their pale wings recalling stitching. “Wonder is the path from the eye to the heart,” reads a page left otherwise blank.

In Drooping Tulip , the stem of a wilting flower tips out of its stoneware bottle and traces a long downward curve. The corolla rests on the table, petals pressed together, a leaf arched above it like a canopy. The image invites the contemplation of a vanitas. Still lifes gain ground from the mid-2010s onward. Hellebore, peonies, quince blossoms, tuberoses — Porzak catches them at every age. The Amaryllis of 2019 opens wide to the lens while others are already giving way.

Based in Los Angeles, Lara Porzak lives with her mother. Marianne Wiggins, a novelist who was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2004 for Evidence of Things Unseen , survived a stroke ten years ago and carries its lasting effects. “The compass of her memory no longer points north,” her daughter observes. “I taped pictures of our loved ones to the walls surrounding her bed to reintroduce her to their faces, so she could remember her own identity.” Views of places they had traveled together joined the walls around her bed, “so she could remember her footprint in the world around her.”

The bottles line the sink where the photographer brushes her teeth: silver nitrate, ferrous sulfate, potassium iodide, cadmium bromide, ethyl ether. At the second sink, her mother’s medications hold the same place — “sentinels of another kind of chemistry,” she says. In the refrigerator, rolls of film sleep between the cheese and the vegetables. “I do not separate my life as a photographer from my daily existence,” she writes. “They are one.”

In the corner of the studio, a hospital bed has been set up for her mother. While her memories fade, Lara Porzak fixes the beauty of the world for them both. In one of her images, crepuscular rays break through the clouds above the Grand Canyon. Epiphany. The book closes on these words: “I will remember.”
The Chemistry of Memory , by Lara Porzak, is published by Damiani , 240 pages, 142 photographs. First edition limited to 1,000 copies, $85 / €75 / £65.
